questions.stem: Examine the EMPLOYEES and NEW_EMPLOYEES tables. Add nonexisting NEW_EMPLOYEES rows to EMPLOYEES and update matching employees’ salaries and job IDs. Which statement does this?

items: 1. Add rows from NEW_EMPLOYEES when the employee does not already exist in EMPLOYEES.
2. For matching employee numbers, modify both SALARY and JOB_ID using values from NEW_EMPLOYEES.

options.text:
MERGE INTO emp_new e
USING new_employees n
ON (n.employee_id = e.employee_id)
WHEN MATCHED THEN INSERT ...
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN UPDATE ...;
options.explanation: The actions are reversed. Matched rows should be updated, while unmatched rows should be inserted.

options.text:
MERGE INTO employees e
USING new_employees n
ON (n.employee_id = e.employee_id)
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET e.salary = n.salary, e.job_id = n.job_id
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (...) VALUES (...);
options.explanation: The matching condition uses the employee ID. Existing employees receive the new salary and job ID, while nonexisting employees are inserted.

options.text:
INSERT INTO employees e
USING new_employees n
ON (n.employee_id = e.employee_id)
WHEN MATCHED ...;
options.explanation: Conditional matched and unmatched processing requires MERGE, not INSERT with this syntax.

options.text: A MERGE statement that updates only SALARY or does not insert all required employee values
options.explanation: The requirements state that both salary and job ID must be updated and unmatched rows must be added.

questions.answerExplanation: The matching condition uses the employee ID. Existing employees receive the new salary and job ID, while nonexisting employees are inserted.

questions.stem: Examine the data in the EMPLOYEES table. Which statement correctly computes the total annual compensation for each employee?

Annual salary plus annual commission, while treating a null commission percentage as zero.

(monthly_salary * 12) +
(monthly_salary * 12 * monthly_commission_pct)
AS annual_comp
FROM employees;

questions.stem: Which two are the minimum requirements for a self-join?

options.text: Only equijoin conditions may be used in the query.
options.explanation: A self-join may use equality or other valid comparison conditions.

options.text: Outer joins must not be used in the query.
options.explanation: A self-join may be implemented as an inner join or an outer join.

options.text: There must be a condition on which the self-join is performed.
options.explanation: A join condition relates rows from one reference of the table to rows from the second reference.

options.text: No other condition except the self-join may be specified.
options.explanation: Additional filtering conditions may be included in the query.

options.text: The table used for the self-join must have two different alias names in the query.
options.explanation: Different aliases distinguish the two references to the same table and allow their columns to be qualified correctly.

questions.stem: Examine the SQL statement used to create the TRANSACTION table. The value A1 does not exist for TM_ID. Which SQL statement successfully inserts a row using the default value for START_DATE?

codeBlocks.title: Table definition

options.text: INSERT INTO transaction VALUES ('A1', DEFAULT, TO_DATE(DEFAULT + 10));
options.explanation: DEFAULT cannot be used as an argument inside TO_DATE and then used in arithmetic as shown.

options.text: INSERT INTO transaction VALUES ('A1', DEFAULT, TO_DATE(SYSDATE + 10));
options.explanation: SYSDATE + 10 already returns a date. Applying TO_DATE to that date introduces an unnecessary implicit conversion.

options.text: INSERT INTO transaction (tm_id, end_date) VALUES ('A1', '10-DEC-2014');
options.explanation: Omitting START_DATE causes its DEFAULT SYSDATE value to be used. A non-null value is supplied for END_DATE.

options.text: INSERT INTO transaction (tm_id, start_date, end_date) VALUES ('A1', '10-DEC-2014');
options.explanation: Three target columns are listed, but only two values are supplied.
